items.q: What does insulin do to blood glucose?
items.correct: It lowers blood glucose by causing cells (especially liver and muscle) to take it up and store it as glycogen.
items.misconception: Insulin raises blood glucose to give the body energy.
items.random_wrong: Insulin destroys glucose in the bloodstream so it cannot be used.
items.why: Students associate sugar with energy and 'doing something with sugar' with raising energy, missing that insulin removes glucose from blood.

items.q: After pre-mRNA splicing in eukaryotes, which sequences remain in the mature mRNA?
items.misconception: Introns remain because they encode the protein; exons are removed as junk.
items.random_wrong: Both introns and exons are removed and the cell uses just the cap and tail.
items.why: Students confuse the EX- (expressed) and IN- prefixes; the naming is the opposite of what intuition suggests.

items.q: What is produced in anaerobic respiration in human muscle cells?
items.correct: Lactic acid (lactate) and a small amount of ATP — no CO2 or water in this pathway.
items.misconception: Anaerobic respiration produces ethanol and CO2 in humans.
items.random_wrong: Anaerobic respiration produces oxygen as a waste product.
items.why: Students confuse anaerobic respiration in yeast (alcohol + CO2) with the human form (lactic acid).

items.q: Is the heart an example of a tissue?
items.correct: No — the heart is an organ made of several tissues (muscle, nervous, epithelial) working together.
items.misconception: The heart is a single tissue.
items.random_wrong: The heart is an organ system on its own.
items.why: Students blur the levels of organisation; a tissue is similar cells, an organ combines tissues, and an organ system combines organs.

items.q: Are specialised cells like red blood cells still able to divide and become other cell types?
items.correct: No — once specialised, most cells cannot become other types; only stem cells are unspecialised and can do this.
items.misconception: Any specialised cell can turn back into a different type of cell.
items.random_wrong: Red blood cells divide rapidly to make all other cell types.
items.why: Students confuse specialised cells with stem cells; differentiation usually commits a cell to its role, while stem cells remain unspecialised.

items.q: Which of these is a prokaryote?
items.why: Correct answer: Bacterium. “Human skin cell” sounds right because it borrows the language of the topic — but it fails this question. Re-read the notes on why.
It's aerobic respiration. “protein synthesis” is the classic near-miss here; knowing why it's wrong is worth as much as knowing the right answer.

items.q: A bacterium is 2 µm long. How many fit end-to-end across a 1 mm gap?
items.why: The real figure is 500 bacteria. The wrong options cluster deliberately close — anchor the exact number to one concrete fact so it can't drift.
